title: Anita Roddick, a Refused Loan and a Green Shop in Brighton
dek: In March 1976 Anita Roddick opened a small shop in Brighton on a £4,000 loan the bank first refused her, to keep her family while her husband was away.

story.event: Borrowing £4,000 and opening the first Body Shop in Brighton
story.summary: On 27 March 1976 Anita Roddick opened the first Body Shop at 22 Kensington Gardens, Brighton, to support herself and her two daughters while her husband Gordon rode from Buenos Aires to New York. The bank refused her a £4,000 loan until she returned with Gordon, and the shop took £130 on its first day. In 1977 she sold half the business for £4,000 to open a second shop in Chichester.
paragraphs: On 27 March 1976 Anita Roddick opened a small shop at 22 Kensington Gardens in Brighton. She had painted it dark green. "The green paint was the only thing that would cover the mould," she later said. Funeral directors nearby objected to a business called The Body Shop; "They went purple with rage when I put the sign up," she recalled. By closing time the shop had taken £130, about half of what she and her husband reckoned it had to earn each week to keep the family.

The shop existed because her husband, Gordon, was leaving to ride horseback from Buenos Aires to New York, a journey of about two years. "It blissed me out to have a partner who said, 'I've got to do this. I've got to be remarkable,'" she said later. She needed a living for herself and their two daughters, and wanted a simple shop she could run from nine to five, home with the girls at night. On her travels she had seen women use ingredients such as cocoa butter on skin and hair, and she was irritated at paying for bulky, expensive packaging.

She needed £4,000. The first time she asked the bank, wearing jeans and a Bob Dylan T-shirt with her daughters beside her, she was turned down. A week later she went back with Gordon, both in suits, and the loan was approved against the couple's hotel. She was relieved, but angry that the manager had spoken to her husband. The products came from a local herbalist and went into the cheapest bottles she could find, the plastic kind hospitals used for urine samples, with handwritten labels. She could not afford enough of them, so she asked customers to bring theirs back for refilling.

Soon she wanted a second shop. The sensible course, she later said, would have been to wait a few years. "But I wasn't the sensible, pragmatic type." The bank would not lend again, so in 1977 she sold half the business for £4,000 to a local garage owner and opened in Chichester. When Gordon returned he suggested franchising, and the company went public in 1984. About fifteen years after Brighton there were around 700 shops.

quote.text: though hitherto I have not been disposed to borrow, knowing that when I had spent what I got I should not be in a condition to repay, I think I can now bring myself to do so in order to raise a fund for these works.
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Aristarchus would not borrow money he could only spend, but agreed to borrow to put his household's skills to work. Roddick's £4,000 was the second kind of debt: a stake on things she already knew how to make and sell, taken before she could know it would pay.

reflection: Roddick's first plan was not an empire. It was a shop she could run from nine to five so that she would be home with her daughters at night, paid for with a loan she had to fight to get. The larger ambition came later, and it grew out of a working week built to fit the life she had.

You are allowed to shape your work that way too. A debt, a new hire or a promise to a client is easier to carry when you know what it is for and what it will ask of your evenings. That is worth deciding before the money or the yes arrives, not after.
invitation: Before you take on the next commitment, whether money, a client or a role, write one sentence on what it is for and one on what it will ask of your evenings. Keep the note where you will see it.

research_notes: Loan: British sources give £4,000; Entrepreneur (2008) gives $6,500 and other American profiles give dollar figures, which appear to be conversions, so the story uses £4,000. The bank story (refused in jeans and a Bob Dylan T-shirt, approved a week later with Gordon, both in suits, against the couple's hotel) is told in most detail by Entrepreneur (1996); the Irish Times confirms that Gordon arranged the loan after Anita failed to convince the bank. First-day takings of £130, half the weekly need, rest on Entrepreneur (1996) alone and are stated as that account gives them. Funeral parlours: the Post Magazine says undertakers across the road objected; the New Zealand Herald says the shop sat between two funeral parlours; the story says only 'funeral directors nearby'. The second-shop investor is called a friend by Entrepreneur (1996) and a local garage owner by the Irish Times; the story uses the Irish Times wording and does not name him. Gordon's ride: Irish Times says a two-year break; the story says about two years. Growth: Brighton & Hove Museums gives around 700 branches about fifteen years after the first shop; Entrepreneur (1996) gave more than 1,400 stores at that date; the story uses the museum's figure for the earlier period. Several quotations ('The green paint...', 'They went purple...') are her later recollections as quoted in obituaries. The repeat screen may meet the surname Roddick in the Big Issue edition: that edition concerns Gordon Roddick, a different person and a different company, so no change was made. The Xenophon passage is Aristarchus's reply after Socrates urges him to set his household of kinswomen to wool-work during the civil strife of 404-403 BC; it is applied here by analogy.
